prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.

text:
On the evening of April 13, 1970, Apollo 13 was about fifty-five hours into its flight, nearly two hundred thousand miles from Earth, when a routine request from Houston changed a lunar mission into a struggle for survival. The spacecraft carried three men: Jim Lovell, a veteran of three earlier flights who was commanding his second trip to the Moon; Jack Swigert, a last-minute replacement for Ken Mattingly, who had been grounded after exposure to German measles; and Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, who had been looking forward to walking on the Moon's Fra Mauro highlands. Mission control asked the crew to stir the oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module, a procedure meant to keep the supercold contents from stratifying.

Swigert flipped the switch, and about ninety seconds later the crew heard a loud bang and felt the spacecraft shudder. Lovell soon radioed the words that became famous in a slightly altered form: "Houston, we've had a problem." Warning lights flashed, the main electrical buses lost power, and the crew could see through a window a gas venting steadily into space. Oxygen tank number two had ruptured, and the explosion had damaged tank number one, leaving the service module with almost no oxygen and, with it, no way to make electricity or water for the command module, Odyssey.

The cause traced back to a chain of small errors made years before the flight. The tank's heater thermostats had been designed for a lower voltage than the ground equipment later supplied. During a pre-launch test the heaters ran far hotter than anyone realised, and they melted the Teflon insulation on the wires inside the tank. When Swigert turned on the stirring fans, a spark from the bare wire ignited the insulation in the pure oxygen, and the pressure rose until the tank failed.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz gathered his White Team and set the tone for what followed. The Moon landing was abandoned almost at once, since nobody could land with a crippled ship, and the only question that mattered was how to get the crew home alive. Odyssey was dying, with its fuel cells starved of oxygen and its batteries meant only for the final hours of reentry. The lunar module, Aquarius, was designed to carry two men for about two days on the Moon's surface, but it had full tanks and working systems. The engineers decided to use it as a lifeboat, and the crew moved into the cramped lander, powering down the command module to save every amp.

The next problem was the route home. Apollo 13 was on a free-return trajectory that would swing around the Moon and bring it back toward Earth, but a recent course change had moved it off that safe path. Controllers wanted to get the crew home quickly, and they chose to fire Aquarius's descent engine, a rocket never intended for such a job, to speed the return. The burn took place shortly after the ship passed behind the Moon, and it shortened the trip to roughly the original schedule. Later, after the ship had rounded the Moon and set off toward Earth, a second burn corrected the trajectory and trimmed the flight time again, so that the ship would splash down in the Pacific on April 17.

Life aboard became a matter of endurance. To conserve power, the crew shut down nearly everything in Aquarius except what was essential, and the cabin temperature dropped toward the freezing point. Condensation ran down the walls, and the men slept little, huddled in the cold with only thin flight suits for warmth. Haise developed a fever from a urinary infection. They also rationed water severely, drinking only a few ounces a day, and became dehydrated, so that Haise's illness and the group's exhaustion worsened as the days passed.

A more immediate danger came from carbon dioxide. Aquarius was equipped with lithium hydroxide canisters to scrub the air, but they were built for two men over a short stay, and they began to fill up. The command module had spare canisters, but they were square while the lander's sockets were round. Engineers on the ground gathered the materials the astronauts had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a spacesuit hose, and duct tape, and within hours they devised a way to fit the square canister to the round receptacle. They read the instructions to the crew, who built the improvised adapter and watched the carbon dioxide level fall back to safe levels. The device became known as the mailbox.

Meanwhile the team on the ground faced the challenge of restarting Odyssey, which had never been designed to be powered up after being shut down so thoroughly. Mattingly, who had been spared the flight by his supposed illness, worked in a simulator with other engineers to write a procedure that would bring the ship back to life using the minimum of electrical power. They had to work out the sequence in a matter of days, and the plan they developed was radioed up to the crew in careful detail. The astronauts also had to navigate manually, since the guidance systems were switched off, and they aligned the ship by sighting on the Sun and Earth, adjusting the course by eye with remarkable precision.

On April 17, the crew prepared to separate from the service module, which they had not been able to see since the accident. When it fell away, they saw for the first time that an entire panel had been blown off and that the side of the vehicle was badly damaged. Lovell reported it to Houston, and the engineers realised how close the explosion had come to destroying the whole spacecraft. The men then jettisoned Aquarius, which had saved them, and said goodbye to it before the lander burned up in the atmosphere.

Reentry brought one last period of suspense. During every Apollo return, radio contact is lost for about three minutes while a sheath of ionised gas surrounds the capsule. This time the blackout stretched beyond that, and the controllers and families waited in silence as the minutes went by. Then, after about four minutes, Swigert's voice came through, and the room erupted. Odyssey descended under its three parachutes and splashed down in the South Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima, shortly after one in the afternoon Houston time.

The crew emerged tired, thin, and unshaven, but alive. The mission was officially termed a successful failure, because the Moon landing was lost but the three men were saved. An investigation board led by Edgar Cortright found the cause in the faulty tank and recommended redesigning the oxygen system, and the changes were made before the flights resumed. Apollo 13 remains remembered as a moment when improvisation, teamwork, and calm under pressure turned a disaster into a rescue, and it showed how much human ingenuity could achieve when the stakes were as high as they could be.
